Proof of False

import Lean
open Lean Elab Command

inductive P : Prop where | mk (b : Bool)
structure C where b : Bool
inductive W : Type where | mk (p : P)
inductive L (α : Type) (b : Bool) : Type where | mk
inductive T : Bool → Prop where | mk : T true

def pad (e : Expr) (n : Nat) : Expr :=
  mkApp (mkLambda `x .default (mkConst ``Nat) e) (.lit (.natVal n))

meta def build : CommandElabM Unit := do
  let f := pad (mkConst ``Bool.false) 78670
  let t := pad (mkConst ``Bool.true) 24083
  unless f.hash == t.hash && f.approxDepth == t.approxDepth do
    throwError "hash collision failed"
  let fw := mkApp (mkConst ``W.mk) (mkApp (mkConst ``P.mk) f)
  let tw := mkApp (mkConst ``W.mk) (mkApp (mkConst ``P.mk) t)
  let w := mkBVar 0
  let Ew := mkApp (mkConst `E) w
  let b := mkProj ``C 0 (mkProj ``C 0 w)
  let l := mkApp2 (mkConst ``L) Ew b
  let Et := mkForall `w .default (mkConst ``W) (mkSort 1)
  let ct := mkForall `w .default (mkConst ``W) <|
    mkForall `l .default l (mkApp (mkConst `E) (mkBVar 1))
  liftCoreM <| addDecl <| .inductDecl [] 1 [{
    name := `E, type := Et, ctors := [{ name := `E.mk, type := ct }] }] false
  let Et := mkApp (mkConst `E) tw
  let l := mkApp2 (mkConst ``L.mk) Et (mkConst ``Bool.true)
  liftCoreM <| addDecl <| .defnDecl {
    name := `e, levelParams := [], type := Et,
    value := mkApp2 (mkConst `E.mk) tw l,
    hints := .abbrev, safety := .safe }
  liftCoreM <| addDecl <| .defnDecl {
    name := `good', levelParams := [],
    type := mkApp (mkConst ``T) t, value := mkConst ``T.mk,
    hints := .abbrev, safety := .safe }
  let Ef := mkApp (mkConst `E) fw
  let Et := mkApp (mkConst `E) tw
  let a := mkApp2 (mkConst `E.mk) fw (mkProj `E 0 (mkConst `e))
  let tl := mkApp2 (mkConst ``L.mk) Et (mkConst ``Bool.true)
  let b := mkApp2 (mkConst `E.mk) tw tl
  let cT := mkApp2 (mkConst ``L) Et t
  let c := mkApp (mkLambda `l .default cT (mkConst ``Unit.unit)) tl
  let fl := mkApp2 (mkConst ``L.mk) Ef f
  let d := mkApp2 (mkConst `E.mk) fw fl
  let v := Expr.letE `a Ef a
    (.letE `b Et b
      (.letE `c (mkConst ``Unit) c
        (.letE `d Ef d (mkConst `good') true) true) true) true
  liftCoreM <| addDecl <| .thmDecl {
    name := `bad, levelParams := [],
    type := mkApp (mkConst ``T) f, value := v }

elab "mkbug" : command => build
mkbug
theorem boom : False := nomatch (bad : T false)
#print axioms bad
#print axioms boom

Re: the question of trust and verification, there are two problems at hand here.

One of them is to give a specification of the kernel, in the form a type system as a bunch of rules, and proving the correctness of the kernel against this specification: the kernel implements a (semi)-decision procedure for this type system. The second is to show meta-theoretic properties of this abstract type system, including building a set-theoretic model or prove consistency by other means.

One would hope these tasks to be largely independent: the first is a program verification problem, the second is a theoretical type theory problem. Sadly, because of the nature of a dependent type checker, one cannot verify the kernel without using a number of difficult to establish theoretical properties. An analogy I like to use is advanced primality tests, which might be relatively easy to implement, but require advanced number theory arguments for their correctness. Still, one could at least reduce verification of the kernel to 1) a set of typing rules 2) a small set of properties these need to satisfy. This would already reduce a lot the "attack surface".

A second issue is that for advanced features like nested inductive types, the type theoretic literature is rather scarce: people typically handle it like @Mario Carneiro's thesis, focusing on a stripped down version of the feature at hand. But that means like bugs like the one at hand are hard to catch because the theory is blind to them. I believe that the solution there is to mechanise the sort of arguments that Mario sketches in his thesis: reducing the complicated inductives from the implementation to a more minimalistic feature amenable to theoretical inquiries.

All of this is a lot of difficult work, at the joint of theory and implementation, but be assured that some of us are very busy at it! On the Lean side, Lean4Lean is the main place where this is happening, but there is also https://metarocq.github.io/ with very similar goals on the Rocq side, and hopefully a lot of knowledge gained on one side should easily transfer to the other.

I don't know the exact state of the art in type theoretical papers about Lean's type theory, but almost all work on type theory for proof assistants makes simplifying assumptions that avoids confronting open questions about extensions to vanilla inductive types that are supported in practice. It's typical to make many simplifying assumptions, just extensions to inductive types are big culprits because some of their nuances are still being worked out type theoretically ATM.

This is just an artifact of the back-and-forth between type theory and pragmatic language design. Type theorists design neat type theoretic features, but people building languages like proof assistants extend those features to make them more useful. Then type theorists scramble to reconcile those extensions with the theory. When they succeed, people implementing new languages have the benefit of hindsight and can build on what is known at the type theory level (hence why Lean was smart enough to use primitive eliminators rather than pattern matching at the kernel level). But they still go on to further improve on usability and, in doing so, introduce new extensions that are not understood yet.

Because of the constancy of this back-and-forth, gaps almost always remain between the theory and the practice that are both interesting and useful. Inductive types and their extensions are pretty recent, so many of those gaps have not been filled yet. (Coinductive types, inductive-inductive types, and so on are even worse culprits because they are even more recent, so the gaps are even larger.) Typically type theory is the slower and less well-funded leg of the two in this back-and-forth, which is why I think we need to support type theoretic research better to make sure we can keep these gaps as small as possible, and close them as quickly as possible.

My big worry right now is that if organizations continue to fund the crap out of AI for formal proof research (and to generally support implementation and maintenance of proof assistants like Lean as part of that effort) but don't bother funding the type theory side of things , those gaps will grow larger and will be exploited more often by AI tools via reward hacking.
